caption: Through-port dip of an all-pass ring: the depth depends on how the coupling r compares with the round-trip loss a; resonances repeat every FSR.
TE modes of a symmetric slab: mode m exists only above its cutoff V = m pi, so V < pi gives a single-mode guide.
Responsivity rises with wavelength (more photons per watt) until the band gap sets a hard long-wavelength cutoff; illustrative eta = 0.8.
Below threshold the diode is a weak LED; above I_th stimulated emission dominates and power rises linearly with current.
Fresnel equations from Maxwell's boundary conditions: p-polarised light is not reflected at the Brewster angle.
At high frequency the field decays inside a conductor over the skin depth, so only a thin surface layer carries current.
Deal-Grove: growth is linear at first (reaction-limited) and slows to parabolic (diffusion-limited) as the oxide thickens.
Why big dies are expensive: with random defects, yield falls exponentially with die area, so smaller chiplets help.
Resolution improves with shorter wavelength and larger NA; the dots mark typical tool settings (idealised, single exposure).
EUV photons carry ~14x more energy, so the same dose delivers far fewer photons per pixel, which makes edges noisier (stochastics).
Square-law model: a resistor-like triode region below V_GS - V_T, then a flat saturation current.
Below threshold the current is exponential in V_GS; the thermal voltage kT/q fixes a ~60 mV/decade floor at room temperature.
A CMOS inverter flips sharply near V_DD/2, restoring logic levels, and draws current only while switching.
Lowering the supply voltage cuts energy quadratically but slows the gates, which is the core dynamic-voltage-scaling trade-off.
The inductor ramps up while the switch is on and down while it is off; the ripple is set by L and the switching frequency.
Duty cycle sets the output: a buck steps down, a boost steps up (with the gain blowing up as D tends to 1), a buck-boost inverts.
Friis free-space loss grows 20 dB per decade of distance and with frequency, which is why mmWave needs high-gain antennas.
Reflection coefficient, return loss and VSWR for a resistive load on a 50 ohm line: only Z_L = Z_0 absorbs everything.
A mass-spring-damper is the model for most MEMS: a high Q gives a tall, narrow resonance, ideal for sensing small shifts.
Proportional control leaves an offset, integral action removes it at the cost of overshoot, and derivative action damps it.
